title: Bank funding and forced-sale risks rise while the estimated capital gap depends heavily on the shock
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
summary: Three of four indicators tracked by New York Fed researchers showed an increasing trend in U.S. banking-system vulnerability through the second quarter of 2026. All remained below the high levels observed before the 2008–09 crisis, although several had moved above the low readings recorded during the following expansion. The distinction matters for interpreting bank credit risk. Banks face losses from selling similar assets, from having too little cash to accommodate withdrawals and from losing capital when securities are repriced. The authors use public bank holding company FR Y-9C filings to model these exposures. Their figures describe the consequences of specified stresses and do not assign probabilities to those stresses.

The starting capital position has weakened modestly since the previous annual update. A top-down model calculates the aggregate dollars required to bring each bank’s Tier 1 common equity to at least 10% of risk-weighted assets after a severe shock. Under conditions replicating the 2007–09 crisis, the gap increased from about $1.9 billion in the second quarter of 2025 to $16.9 billion a year later. Under a repeat of the 2022 interest-rate shock, the gap was considerably larger at $151.1 billion, although lower year over year. The text gives the earlier figure as $161.3 billion, while the companion chart data show $165.23 billion for the same quarter. Either reading gives the same direction. The rate scenario fully recognizes unrealized gains and losses on both available-for-sale and held-to-maturity securities. The starting-capital chart shows the reported capital ratio falling from 13.01% to 12.42%, while the ratio after recognition of unrealized marks changed from 11.10% to 11.05%.

A forced-sale exercise measures a different exposure. A common decline in asset values leads banks to sell to reduce leverage. Those sales depress prices for other holders. Estimated spillover losses rose from approximately 14.0% to 15.7% of Tier 1 capital between the two second quarters. Securities and capital are marked to fair value for this calculation. The decomposition attributes much of the rise beginning in 2022 and the subsequent movements to leverage. System size relative to other financial institutions and overlap in exposures also enter the model (fire-sale index and decomposition).

The liquidity stress ratio rose from approximately 0.470 to 0.484 over the year, reaching a level last seen in 2014. It weights liabilities and off-balance-sheet obligations by assumed outflow rates and assets by how readily they can be liquidated. The system measure is a size-weighted average of bank ratios. The rise since early 2022 combined fewer liquid assets with more unstable funding and off-balance-sheet exposure. The latest reading was still only slightly above half the 2007 peak. Its increase measures a growing mismatch under the assumed stress, distinct from a cash shortfall actually experienced.

The run model links liquidity and solvency. A simultaneous asset shock and loss of funding forces costly sales. Its index measures the minimum fraction of unstable funding that a bank must retain to remain solvent in that scenario. The size-weighted figure rose from 0.26 to 0.31 in a year. A higher threshold means the institution can withstand less funding flight. More illiquid assets, less stable funding and higher stress leverage all contributed (run-vulnerability decomposition). Because the four exercises use different shocks and units, summing their outputs would double-count related exposures and obscure which assumptions drive each result.

questions.question: Which banks account for the capital shortfall under the rate scenario?
questions.detail: The modeled gap is much larger when unrealized securities marks are recognized. Aggregate starting ratios reveal little about the banks that fall furthest below 10%. Use contemporaneous bank holding company FR Y-9C filings, securities footnotes and the cited CLASS model documentation to reconstruct the distribution. Concentration in a handful of institutions would imply different issuer-level credit exposure than a broadly shared decline.

questions.question: Would a plausible change in funding behaviour materially alter the estimated run threshold?
questions.detail: The model requires retention of a larger share of unstable funding, while the liquidity measure uses assumed outflow and asset-liquidity weights. Examine bank regulatory filings and public liquidity disclosures for deposit concentrations, unused commitments, secured funding and unencumbered liquid assets. Recompute sensitivities under common outflow assumptions. The result would help distinguish institutions with similar capital marks but very different capacity to meet near-term cash needs.

questions.question: How much would an attempted sale actually depress the price of assets held across banks?
questions.detail: The fire-sale exercise assumes a common asset shock followed by deleveraging. Its capital loss depends on market depth and the holdings other institutions share. Compare the cited model’s price-impact assumptions with regulatory securities schedules and transaction or dealer-volume records available at the assessment date. Assessing the overlap and likely execution costs would help size secondary losses beyond the original rate shock.
